## Guwahati Railway Station — production brief

**Location and layout**
- Guwahati Railway Station is station code **GHY**, on Station Road in **Mawhati/Paltan Bazaar, Guwahati, Kamrup Metropolitan district**, at approximately **59 m elevation**. It is part of Northeast Frontier Railway and falls under the Lumding Division.
- The station is an active, at-grade railway hub with **seven platforms** and electrified rail infrastructure. The ASTC bus terminal is located at the rear of the station; taxis, autos, e-rickshaws and parking serve the wider station area.
- It is an urban station rather than a controlled backlot. An NFR inspection record reported more than **40,000 daily passengers** in 2018, along with waiting rooms, tea stalls on multiple platforms, security arrangements, lifts/escalators, vehicle bays and local-cultural artwork on station walls.

**Entrances and redevelopment**
- NFR stated in 2023 that the station had historically operated with one entrance on the north/Pan Bazar side. A second entrance from the Paltan Bazaar/ASTC side, plus a roof plaza and upgraded facilities, was planned as part of redevelopment.
- A September 2025 report described a larger redevelopment plan with two entry gates. The available evidence does not confirm that every planned entrance, roof-plaza feature or upgraded facility is operational on the shoot date. Treat the entrance configuration as a recce item, not a fixed assumption.

**Permissions and restrictions**
- For an Indian production, the relevant authority is the **Chief Public Relations Officer of Northeast Frontier Railway**. NFR’s public directory lists CPRO **Kapinjal K. Sharma** and office numbers **+91 9957550020, 0361-2676085 and 0361-2671448**.
- Feature films, television/web shows and series can use the Film Facilitation Office single-window route. Documentaries, music videos and AV commercials are directed to apply to the Railways rather than through that feature-film route.
- The application should identify the exact station/areas, proposed dates, purpose, detailed railway-scene script and shooting schedule. Railway review covers safe normal operations and railway security. Station, train and route names cannot be changed or masked without specific approval.
- Expect a licence fee, case-specific security deposit, comprehensive insurance, indemnity agreement and safety/security conditions. A Publicity liaison officer is required; feature films may also have Commercial and Security liaison officers.
- Railway rules prohibit filming from footboards or rooftops and prohibit filming on tracks while a train is moving. The team must not obstruct passengers or normal railway operations. The guidelines specifically advise avoiding daytime shooting at crowded stations, making a night schedule more practical for this scene, subject to railway approval.

**Scene-specific recommendations**
- **Crowd extras:** Request a defined, cordoned filming zone on one platform or in the circulating area. Keep passenger routes, stairways, escalators, platform edges and emergency access clear. Because the station remains operational, plan extras and camera moves around live passenger flow rather than attempting to control the whole platform.
- **Train approaching:** Do not put actors, extras, camera equipment or crew on the track. For real-train footage, submit the exact platform, safe camera position, train identity and timing for operational approval. A safer production design is to capture a permitted long-lens arrival plate from behind the platform safety line and supplement it with stock footage, sound design or VFX if required.
- **Lighting and signage:** Preserve authentic station signage and train identities unless the written permission expressly allows alterations. The redevelopment plan mentions modern signage, but the available sources do not establish current platform lighting levels or fixture types. Conduct a night recce for practical light direction, shadow, glare, platform-number visibility and power access; obtain approval before adding or rigging supplementary lights.
- **Access/logistics:** Confirm which entrance is open for crew load-in, where production vehicles may wait, whether parking is available for the permitted unit, and the route from the entrance to the selected platform. Include RPF/railway liaison time, passenger-management staff, weather protection for equipment and a strict equipment footprint in the schedule.
- **Weather:** The IMD Guwahati observation on 18 August 2026 recorded **32°C and 79% humidity** at 17:30 IST. For any August shoot, protect cameras, sound gear and lighting from rain and check the official forecast for the actual night.

**Bottom line:** The station can deliver a convincing crowded, active Northeast-Indian railway setting, but the scene should be planned as a live operational railway shoot: obtain NFR permission early, recce the exact platform and entrance, use a railway-approved safe position for the train shot, and treat current redevelopment and lighting details as unconfirmed until verified on site.

research_findings.output:
## Kaziranga filming brief — current position: 18 August 2026

**Immediate feasibility:** Do not schedule principal photography inside the park on 18 August without written confirmation. A 2026 closure notice states that visitor access ended on 29 May for the monsoon, and standard visitor information describes June–September as the closed period. The official booking site simultaneously displays “open daily,” so the production should obtain current written clearance from the Director/Field Director before travel; unauthorized entry is prohibited.

**Location and visual context:** Kaziranga is a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Assam’s Brahmaputra floodplain. Its landscape combines forest, tall elephant grass, reeds, marshes, shallow pools and wet alluvial grasslands. Seasonal flooding, erosion and changing water bodies are part of the environment. The park is also a Tiger Reserve and is managed by the Assam Forest Department.

**Permits and approvals:**
- Treat this as protected-area filming, not ordinary location photography. Park rules prohibit entering areas without appropriate permission.
- For feature films, TV/web shows and reality productions, India Cine Hub describes an online application with a non-refundable fee equivalent to USD 225. Prepare the script/synopsis, crew passport details, locations and dates, and equipment list. Normal processing is stated as up to three weeks, with longer timelines possible where additional government consultations are required.
- The India Cine Hub route does not accept documentary films, AV commercials or music videos; those formats need a separate clearance route through the park/forest authorities.
- The permission letter may facilitate local permissions but does not necessarily replace direct permission from Kaziranga’s authorities. The listed park contact is the Director, Kaziranga National Park: dir.kaziranganp@gmail.com.
- Because Kaziranga is a Tiger Reserve, confirm that the proposed trail is not core or critical tiger habitat. A current filming-permission guide states that filming is not permitted in core/critical habitat and that any permitted buffer filming is regulated. Confirm crew size, vehicles, equipment, escort, route, hours and wildlife-distance conditions in writing.

**Trail accessibility:** A government filming-location listing describes an approximately 5 km Nature Trail in the Burapahar range. Separate visitor information identifies the Kukurkata trail as an 11 km round trip and says Panbari’s 5 km route is closed. These descriptions are not fully consistent, so a walking scene should be tied to a specifically approved trail and ranger/park supervision rather than assumed to be available with a normal jeep-safari booking.

**Timing and mist:** The official site lists park hours from 7:00 a.m. to sunset/5:00 p.m.; its scheduled morning visitor trip is 7:30–10:00 a.m. Jeep access is listed for all four principal ranges: Kohora, Bagori, Agaratoli and Burapahar. Visitor information describes November–February as mild and dry, with daytime temperatures generally below 25°C and nights potentially as low as 7°C. This is the most promising period for a cool morning look, but natural mist is not guaranteed and should be confirmed by a recce. Any artificial haze, smoke or atmospheric equipment should be pre-cleared; avoid anything that could disturb wildlife.

**Operational restrictions:** The park’s published rules require biodegradable materials, removal/deposit of waste, silence around animals, reporting of injured wildlife and a 20 km/h vehicle limit. Production guidance for Indian forests additionally recommends no off-road driving, no open fire, no disturbing artificial light or sound, and separate approval for drones. Keep the unit small, carry only approved equipment, and plan all movement around the ranger’s route and timing instructions.

**Access and base logistics:** Kohora is the main tourist hub on NH-37. The official access information gives approximate road transfers of 250 km/5 hours from Guwahati, 105 km/2 hours from Jorhat Airport and 90 km/2 hours from Tezpur. India Cine Hub lists Jorhat’s Rowriah Airport about 90 km away and Furkating Railway Station about 80 km away. Build substantial contingency for monsoon flooding, road conditions, wildlife controls and restricted park hours.

**Indicative official park charges:** The published schedule lists, per day, feature-film fees of ₹100,000 for Indian productions and ₹200,000 for foreign productions; documentary-film fees of ₹15,000 and ₹75,000 respectively; matching security deposits; and professional movie/video-camera charges of ₹10,000 and ₹30,000 respectively. Confirm the applicable range, production category and current tariff directly before budgeting.

**Practical recommendation:** If the scene must show Rahul walking, first pursue an approved Burapahar/Kukurkata trail option during the open season. If the permit authority will not allow a crew on an in-park trail, reproduce the misty forest look in an authorized buffer/territorial forest location or controlled set rather than assuming that a standard safari ticket permits pedestrian filming.

**Supporting sources:** Official Kaziranga National Park & Tiger Reserve website; India Cine Hub/Kaziranga location listing; UNESCO World Heritage Centre; Assam visitor information; Indian-forest filming-permission guidance.

sources.title: Kaziranga National Park - UNESCO World Heritage Centre
excerpts: River bank erosion, sedimentation and formation of new lands as well as new water-bodies, plus succession between grasslands and woodlands represents outstanding examples of significant and ongoing, dynamic ecological and biological processes. Wet alluvial grasslands occupy nearly two-thirds of the park area and are maintained by annual flooding and burning. These natural processes create complexes of habitats which are also responsible for a diverse range of predator/prey relationships. **Criterion (x):** Kaziranga was inscribed for being the world’s major stronghold of the Indian one-horned rhino, having the single largest population of this species, currently estimated at over 2,000 animals. The property also provides habitat for a number of globally threatened species including tiger, Asian elephant, wild water buffalo, gaur, eastern swamp deer, Sambar deer, hog deer, capped langur, hoolock gibbon and sloth bear. ... The park’s location at the junction of the Australasia and Indo-Asian flyway means that the park’s wetlands play a crucial role for the conservation of globally threatened migratory bird species. The Endangered Ganges dolphin is also found in some of the closed oxbow lakes. ... The introduction of rinderpest and domestic buffaloes has had negative effects on the wild water buffalo population, including hybridisation and genetic swamping of the remaining wild stock. Poaching of rhino has been a serious problem but the overall population levels are steady or rising. Another issue is seasonal flooding which causes many animals to migrate outside the park where they are susceptible to hunting and reprisal for crop damage. The presence of the busy national highway No. 37 along the southern border of Kaziranga has brought increased settlements which disturb wildlife movements in this landscape. While river migration has also resulted in the loss of some 5,000 ha of forest land from 1925 to 1986, the national park has been enlarged to the north to include part of the River Brahmaputra, although this area has not yet been proposed for inclusion within the World Heritage property. ... The property receives the highest legal protection and strong legislative framework under the provisions of the Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 and Indian Forest Act, 1927/Assam Forest Regulation 1891. The park has a long history of protection for over a century, reflected in the dramatic recovery of the rhino. The park has been declared as a Tiger Reserve in 2007 and there have been six additions to the park area which has improved management and protection efforts. The property benefits from government support at both national and regional levels as well as involvement of national and international conservation organisations. The site is managed under the administration of the Assam Forest Department, guided by a legally approved Management Plan. The present state of protection and conservation of the property is regarded as one of the best in India. However, key threats include rhino poaching, riverbank erosion, invasive species, tourism pressure, heavy highway traffic, and livestock grazing (particularly in the areas which have been added to the park). The management needs a long-term strategy for dealing with tourism-related issues, research and monitoring for habitat and wildlife, human-wildlife conflicts and boundary issues relating to the addition areas to the national park.

Normally, jeep safari inside Kaziranga National Park lasts for maximum 2 (two) hours. \*\*\* Click here to know the Kaziranga National Park Photo Gallery Kaziranga Jeep Safari Routes **Central Range (Kohora)** Mihimukh -- Kathpora -- Daphlang -- Diphlu River Bank -- Mona Beel -- Karasing & return **Western Range (Bagori)** Donga beel -- Roumari -- Raja Pukhuri -- Mona Beel & return **Eastern Range (Agaratoli)** Agaratoli -- Sohola Beel -- Rang Gaon Motia -- Maklung -- Turturoni -- Dhoba & return **Burhapahar Range (Ghorakati)** Ghorakati -- Potahi Beel -- Diphlu -- Phulaguri -- Tunikati & return Kaziranga Trekking Routes **Kukurkata Reserve Forest** Kukurkata Reserve Forest under Burhapahar range is the most popular and only trek open for visitors. sources.title: Filming in Indian Forests: Permission Toolkit
excerpts: Reserved and Protected Forests; first point of application State Chief Wildlife Warden / PCCF (Wildlife); Principal Secretary (Forest) National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries Central, tiger reserves NTCA, under MoEFCC Tiger Reserves (buffer only) Central, parks MoEFCC Wildlife Division National Parks clearance Foreign crews Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), then the above Any public or commercial release **Hard limit:** the core or critical tiger habitat of a Tiger Reserve is inviolate under Section 38V of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 (as amended 2006). No film shooting is permitted there. Productions work the buffer zones and territorial forest divisions instead. **2\. Land Classification and What It Controls** Identify the legal status of every location first. It decides the authority, the lead time and whether filming is allowed at all. **Classification Status Permission route** Reserved Forest (RF) Highest protection under the Indian Forest Act State Forest Dept (DFO / division) Protected Forest (PF) Protected, some local rights State Forest Dept Unclassed / village forest Lighter restriction Local forest division Wildlife Sanctuary Protected Area, WLPA 1972 Chief Wildlife Warden National Park Protected Area, WLPA 1972 Chief Wildlife Warden + MoEFCC Tiger Reserve Core inviolate; buffer regulated NTCA + state (buffer only) Conservation / Community Reserve Protected Area Chief Wildlife Warden Eco-Sensitive Zone (ESZ) Up to 10km around parks/sanctuaries Regulated activity, check notification **3\. Pre-Production Forest Permit Checklist** Classify every location (RF / PF / Sanctuary / National Park / Tiger Reserve / ESZ), which sets the authority track Confirm no location sits in core or critical tiger habitat (filming prohibited there) Application in the prescribed form to the jurisdictional Range Officer / ACF / DFO / Chief Wildlife Warden MoEFCC Wildlife Division clearance for National Parks; NTCA approval for Tiger Reserve buffer shoots MEA clearance for foreign crews where the film is for public broadcast or commercial release **lineproducersindia.in** A Celluloid Pact brand Page 1 of 2 **PRE-PRODUCTION TOOLKIT** Eco-Sensitive Zone check for any location within about 10km of a park or sanctuary Separate DGCA Digital Sky drone permission; verify the area is not a no-fly zone for aerial work Wildlife protocol plan: crew, vehicle and equipment caps, forest-staff escort, distance from fauna, daylight-only where required Fees, camera fee, vehicle entry and guide or escort charges confirmed against the division's current schedule Security deposit lodged; indemnity, insurance, fire and waste-removal undertakings signed Approved permit and IDs carried on site; forest-staff escort confirmed before the unit moves **4\. Fees and Cost Worksheet** Forest and park fees are set by each state Forest Department and individual park, and they vary widely, so budget against the jurisdiction's current schedule rather than a national figure. The cost lines that recur: **Cost line Basis** Commercial filming fee Per day, by park / division and production type (feature, OTT, documentary, ad) Camera fee Per camera per day Vehicle entry Per vehicle per day Guide / escort charges Mandatory forest-staff escort, per day Security deposit Refundable after wrap, no damage Foreign-crew surcharge Where applicable, plus MEA / MoEFCC processing **Documentaries vs features:** wildlife documentaries are often treated more favourably than commercial features, but both follow the same authority chain. Build the multi-agency lead time (state Forest Dept, plus MoEFCC and NTCA for parks and tiger reserves) into the schedule from the start. **5\. Wildlife and Eco-Sensitive Compliance** Forest permits come with conservation conditions, and a breach can halt the shoot or bar future access. The non-negotiables: No filming in core or critical tiger habitat, kept inviolate under the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 Respect Eco-Sensitive Zone restrictions on regulated activities around parks and sanctuaries No off-road driving, no feeding or baiting, maintain the prescribed distance from wildlife Crew, vehicle and equipment numbers capped to the permit; forest-staff escort at all times No artificial lighting or sound that disturbs fauna; many parks are daylight-only Drones only with DGCA Digital Sky clearance and park permission; most protected areas are no-fly No plastic, no waste, no open fire; carry out all material and restore the site Follow the Range Officer's instructions on access, timing and routes without exception **6\.

excerpts: Its on the National Highway 37 (NH 37) which is linked to Guwahati on the west and Jorhat on the east. From Guwahati, it can directly be reached by road (NH 37). It takes anything from 4-5 hours depending upon time of travel and traffic congestion. The route from Guwahati is Guwahati – Sonapur – Khetri – Jagiroad – Nelli – Dharamtul – Nagaon (bypass) – Puranigodam – Samaguri – Kaliabor Tiniali (junction from where one can divert to Tezpur) – Jakhlabandha – Burapahar (Ghorakati) – Bagori – Kohora. From Golaghat: Kohora can be reached from Golaghat (and further south from Dimapur which 85 km south of Golaghat on NH39, and Diphu which is about 120 km from Golaghat). Move northward on NH39 from Golaghat till Numaligarh -NH37 Tri-Junction. from the triple point take a left turn on the NH 37. Golaghat to Kohora distance is about 50 km. From Silchar: From Silchar one can take the National Highway 54 and reach Nagaon (Bypass) via Bandarkhal – Jatinga – Haflong – Mahur – Maibang – Lumding – Doboka – Kathiatoli. By Road from Shillong: One can reach Kohora from Shillong via Jorabat (which is 80 km from Shillong on the NH 40). Enroute one would pass via Nongpoh and Umling. From Jorabat, one can turn right on the NH37 and follow the road via Sonapur – Khetri – Jagiroad – Nelli – Dharamtul – Nagaon (bypass) – Puranigodam – Samaguri – Kaliabor Tiniali (junction from where one can divert to Tezpur) – Jakhlabandha – Burapahar (Ghorakati) – Bagori – Kohora. |Route |STARTING POINT |DESTINATION |TRANSPORT |DISTANCE |DURATION | |**Route 1** |Lokpriya Gopinath Bordoloi International Airport, Borjhar, Guwahati |Kaziranga (Kohora) |By road (NH37) |250 Kms |5 hrs | |**Route 2** |Rowroya Airport, Jorhat |Kaziranga (Kohora) |By road (NH37) |105 Kms |2 hrs | |**Route 3** |Guwahati Railway Station |Kaziranga (Kohora) |By road (NH37) |210 Kms |4 hrs | |**Route 4** |Tezpur |Kaziranga (Kohora) |By road (NH37) |90 Kms |2 hrs | Contact info Kaziranga National Park, NH-37, P.O Bokakhat, Golaghat, Assam 785612 + kazirangabooking@gmail.com + \+917099074676 03776 268007 + [](https://www.facebook.com/KazirangaNP?mibextid=ZbWKwL) [](https://twitter.com/kaziranga_) [](https://www.instagram.com/kaziranganptr_official/) Quick Links Guwahati has regular flights to and from Delhi, Kolkata, Imphal, Agartalla, Bagdogra, Dibrugarh, Silchar and Jorhat.
